t.4.18.1: Thus was Rāma addressed by the stricken, half-conscious Vālin in words that were harsh, yet courteous, salutary, and in keeping with dharma and artha.
t.4.18.2: Him, the best of monkeys, who had spoken his words and now was like a sun bereft of radiance, like a cloud that has released its water, like a fire that has died down,
t.4.18.3: Reproached in this way, Rāma then spoke in reply to Vālin, the unsurpassed lord of the monkeys, who was endowed with dharma, artha and virtues.
t.4.18.4: Without understanding dharma, artha and kāma, or even worldly convention, how can you, out of childishness, censure me here today?
t.4.18.6: This earth, with its mountains, woods and forests, belongs to the Ikṣvākus, and so too do the punishment and the favour of beasts, birds and men.
t.4.18.5: Without consulting the elders who are endowed with wisdom and esteemed by teachers, O gentle one, you wish, out of a monkey's fickleness, to lecture me here.
t.4.18.7: That land is protected by Bharata, righteous of soul, truthful in speech and upright, who knows the true essence of dharma, kāma and artha, and is devoted to restraining and to showing favour.
t.4.18.8: He in whom both sound policy and discipline, as well as truth, are firmly established, and in whom valor is seen as it ought to be, that king knows the proper place and time.
t.4.18.9: Bound by his righteous command, we and others of royal rank roam the entire earth, desiring the continuance of dharma.
t.4.18.11: We, therefore, standing firm in our own supreme duty and placing Bharata's command before us, punish according to the prescribed rule one who has strayed from the path.
t.4.18.10: O tiger among kings, while Bharata, devoted to dharma, protects the whole earth, who could act to suppress dharma?
t.4.18.12: But you are one whose dharma is corrupted, you are condemned by your own deeds, you are ruled chiefly by lust, and you have not kept to the path of kings.
t.4.18.13: The elder brother, the father, and the one who imparts knowledge: these three are to be known as fathers, as long as they abide in dharma and keep to the right path.
t.4.18.14: A younger brother, one's own son, and a pupil distinguished by virtue: these three are to be regarded as sons, if dharma is the guiding principle here.
t.4.18.15: Subtle and exceedingly hard to know is the dharma of the good, O monkey. The self, dwelling in the heart of all beings, knows what is good and what is evil.
t.4.18.16: Fickle yourself, taking counsel with fickle monkeys of undisciplined mind, like one born blind consulting with those born blind, what indeed will you see?
t.4.18.17: But I shall tell you plainly the meaning of these words: you ought not to censure me merely out of anger.
t.4.18.18: See now this reason for which you have been slain by me: abandoning the eternal dharma, you live with your brother's wife.
t.4.18.19: While this great-souled Sugrīva is still living, you, doer of sinful deeds, out of lust consort with Rumā, who stands to you as a daughter-in-law.
t.4.18.20: Therefore, O monkey, since you strayed from dharma and acted from lust, this punishment has been meted out to you for this violation of your brother's wife.
t.4.18.21: For one who is opposed to dharma and has strayed from the accepted conduct of the world, I see no means of restraint other than punishment, O leader of the monkey troops.
t.4.18.22: The man who, driven by lust, approaches his own sister, or the wife of his younger brother, is held by tradition to deserve death as his punishment.
t.4.18.23: Bharata is the lord of the earth, and we are those who carry out his commands; and you have strayed from dharma, so how could you be overlooked?
t.4.18.24: The wise Bharata, ruling in accordance with dharma, stands resolved to restrain one who has transgressed the dharma owed to elders, and all those who live by lust.
t.4.18.25: But we, O lord of the monkeys, taking Bharata's command as our rule, stand ready to restrain those like you who have broken the bounds of propriety.
t.4.18.26: My friendship with Sugrīva is just like my friendship with Lakṣmaṇa, and for the sake of his wife and his kingdom he is devoted to my highest good.
t.4.18.27: And at that time I gave my promise in the presence of the monkeys; how could a promise be disregarded by one such as I?
t.4.18.28: Therefore, for all these great reasons bound up with dharma, may you acknowledge that the punishment dealt to you was fitting.
t.4.18.29: In every way your punishment must be regarded as nothing but dharma by one who sees the help owed to a friend as dharma itself.
t.4.18.30: But men who have committed sins and have received punishment from kings become free of stain and go to heaven, just like the good who have done righteous deeds.
t.4.18.31: My noble ancestor Māndhātṛ ordained a terrible punishment when a śramaṇa had committed a sin just like the sin you have committed.
t.4.18.32: Sin has been committed by other heedless lords of the earth as well, and they perform expiation; by that, the taint is quelled.
t.4.18.33: Therefore enough of this anguish; the slaying was ordained in accordance with dharma, O tiger among monkeys. We are not masters of our own will.
t.4.18.34: With nets, with snares and with various traps, men, whether hidden or in plain view, capture a great many animals, whether they are fleeing or terrified, trusting or standing quite still.
t.4.18.35: Men who eagerly seek meat strike down animals whether they are heedless or watchful, and even when they are turned away, and no fault is found in this.
t.4.18.36: Royal sages who know dharma also go hunting in this world. Therefore, O monkey, you were struck down by me with an arrow in battle, whether you were fighting back or not, for you are only a beast of the branches.
t.4.18.37: Kings, O best of monkeys, are without doubt the bestowers of dharma, which is hard to attain, and of an auspicious life.
t.4.18.38: One should not harm them, nor revile them, nor insult them, nor speak anything unpleasant to them; for these are gods who move about upon the surface of the earth in human form.
t.4.18.39: But you, without understanding dharma, giving yourself over to anger alone, revile me, who stand firm in the dharma handed down from my fathers and forefathers.
t.4.18.40: Thus addressed by Rāma, Vālī, the lord of the monkeys, deeply distressed, then replied to Rāma with joined palms.
t.4.18.41: What you have said, O best of men, is exactly so; there is no doubt about it. For an inferior one cannot answer back to one who is superior.
t.4.18.42: Whatever improper and unpleasant words were spoken by me earlier out of heedlessness, even for that, O Rāghava, you surely ought not to hold it as a fault of mine.
t.4.18.43: For you know the true essence of things as they are seen, and you are devoted to the welfare of the people. In accomplishing what must be done and its means, your mind is clear and unfailing.
t.4.18.45: But Vālī, his throat choked with tears, gazing at Rāma, spoke slowly in a pained voice, like an elephant sunk fast in mire.
t.4.18.44: O knower of dharma, protect me too with words that accord with dharma, though I have strayed from dharma and given transgression the foremost place.
t.4.18.46: I do not grieve for myself, nor for Tārā, nor even for my kinsmen, as I grieve for my son Aṅgada, foremost in virtues, who wears golden armlets.
t.4.18.47: He who has been fondly cherished since childhood, made wretched by no longer seeing me, will waste away like a pond whose water has been drunk dry.
t.4.18.48: Turn your finest regard toward Sugrīva and toward Aṅgada as well, for you are their ruler and their protector, established in deciding what ought and ought not to be done.
t.4.18.49: O lord of men, the conduct you show toward Bharata and toward Lakṣmaṇa, O king, that same conduct you ought to consider showing toward Sugrīva and Aṅgada.
t.4.18.50: You should act in such a way that Sugrīva does not scorn poor Tārā, who has been made to share in guilt through the faults committed by me.
t.4.18.51: For it is only by one who has been favoured by you, who stays under your control and follows your wishes, that the kingdom can be ruled.
t.4.18.52: Then Rāma consoled him, Vālin, whose vision had now become clear.
t.4.18.53: You need not be anxious about us, nor about yourself, O best of monkeys; we have firmly resolved, in accordance with dharma, to act with special regard for you.
t.4.18.54: He who inflicts punishment upon one deserving of punishment, and he who, deserving punishment, is punished, both have accomplished their purpose in respect of the deed and its cause, and neither of them comes to ruin.
t.4.18.55: Therefore, through this union with punishment, you, freed from your sin, have returned to your own righteous nature by the path that dharma has shown.
t.4.18.56: Having heard the sweet and well-composed words of the great-souled Rāma, who followed the path of dharma and crushed his foes in battle, the vānara spoke a fitting reply.
t.4.18.57: O lord, that I, burning from your arrow and out of my senses, reviled you in my ignorance, forgive me this, O you whose fearsome valor equals great Indra's; be appeased, O lord of the earth.
